newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Daimler-Benz moves back into profit.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Daimler-Benz moves back into profit.

text.p: Daimler-Benz AG, Germany's largest industrial group, marked its first step towards financial recovery on Thursday, posting a 2.4 billion mark ($1.6 billion) rebound in first-half net earnings after record losses in 1995.

Daimler, whose savage restructuring programme plunged it into a 5.7 billion mark loss last year, said net profits in the first six months of 1996 surged to 782 million marks from a 1.6 billion mark loss in the first half of 1995.

Management board chairman Juergen Schrempp told a London news conference that he expected the group's profit in the second half of the year to be at least as high as profits in the first half. But he emphasised that while results were vastly improved, they were still "way off" company targets.

"So let there be no mistake. We have only just begun," Schrempp said. "Our goal remains that each business unit will achieve a return that is among the top of the world class companies in each sector where we compete."

Group sales climbed nine percent to 49.07 billion marks as operating profits swung to a 827 million mark profit from a 613 million mark loss. The turnaround was mainly fueled by Daimler's flagship unit, truck and luxury car maker Mercedes-Benz AG.
Daimler wants all its businesses to increase the return on capital employed to 12 percent, a target that Chief financial officer Manfred Gentz said would be met in 1998 or 1999.

Schrempp hinted that the results, which were released in London according to U.S. GAAP accounting principles to boost transparency and stimulate global awareness, may enable the group to pay a dividend this year if profits are sustained.
"We will go back to discuss dividends," he said.
Daimler-Benz paid no dividend in 1995.

Although net profits were at the top end of analysts' expectations, Daimler shares -- which had been climbing over the last few days in anticipation of strong numbers -- slipped two pfennigs to 81.30 marks on profit-taking, traders said.

But analysts in Frankfurt, who noted the profits were helepd by a tax credit rather than a charge, said they may nudge up forecasts. "They are on their way to attaining more reasonable levels of profitability," said Bob Barber of HSBC James Capel.

Daimler's profits were led by Mercedes-Benz despite depressed European market conditions for trucks. Mercedes, helped by a stronger dollar and booming sales of its E-Class car, posted a 2.8 percent profit rise to 1.4 billion marks.
"Mercedes is now the most profitable automobile manufacturer in the world on a per unit basis and we intend to keep it that way," Schrempp said.
Daimler-Benz Aerospace (DASA), in the midst of a massive cost cutting campaign, narrowed its operating loss to 677 million marks from 1.62 billion marks in the first-half of 1995.

Schrempp reiterated that DASA would reach break even by 1998, saying he was encouraged by overall growth in the global aircraft industry and a record inflow of Airbus orders. DASA is a major partner in the Airbus Industrie consortium.
But he denied that Daimler planned to demerge the troubled division when it had broken back into the black.
Daimler-Benz InterServices (Debis), the financial and services division, saw operating profits climb to 212 million marks from 156 million marks in the year earlier period.
Daimler fell into deep losses last year as it undertook a massive reorganisation aimed at returning it to its transportation roots and abandoning dreams to become an integrated technology company.
In 1995, it took one-off charges of 3.9 billion marks, including a 2.3 billion mark writedown of Dutch aircraft maker Fokker NV and 1.6 billion marks for streamlining its AEG unit.
Schrempp said Daimler had cut the number of business units in the group's portfolio to 25 from 35 since last May.
"The earnings potential for the steamlined portfolio has increased substantially," he said. ($1=1.4770 Mark)
